parents.outro: Most parents want to know what is happening and how to help. Give them a role and they will take it.

B1.tagline: Look up. Open your body. Shoot when you can.
B1.overview: This block builds the individual habits every other block depends on: looking before the ball arrives, opening the body to the field, using the first touch to go forward, and shooting. At U10 the ball also comes under pressure, so the touch has to work with an opponent close by.

B2.tagline: Pass, move, and be an option.
B2.overview: This is where passing becomes a tool. Players learn that a teammate can solve a problem a dribble cannot. The first habit is the give and go: pass, then move to a new spot to receive again. The second is the 2v1: recognize when a teammate is free and use them to beat a defender.

B3.tagline: Close the ball. Cover your teammate.
B3.overview: Defending is a team job. At U10 this block introduces the idea that the nearest player pressures the ball, the next player covers, and the team stays close together. The aim is to stop the opponent from playing forward and win the ball back as high up the field as possible.

who.label: They have been around the game
who.text: Most of these players have been playing for several years. They are still developing their understanding that passing creates space and that defending takes real collective effort. They are ready to be coached on how their individual actions connect to what the team is doing.

who.label: How you deliver feedback matters

who.label: Two practices build habits
who.text: With two sessions a week, what you introduce on day one has time to settle before day two builds on it. Pay attention to what shows up in the second session without you asking for it. That carry-over is the sign the concept is taking hold.

who.label: Ask them why, not just what
who.text: Players at this age can answer deeper questions. "Why does switching the ball make the defender's job harder?" is a question a U12 player can genuinely engage with. Use that.

great_session.title: Immediate reaction to transition
great_session.text: When the ball turns over, do players react instantly? Or do they watch it happen? That first-second reaction is the whole introduction to the game-moments block.

great_session.title: Compact defending shape
great_session.text: Are defenders close enough to support each other? The distance between first and second defender tells you everything about their shape.

great_session.title: Combination play happening naturally
great_session.text: Players who are passing and moving without being asked are showing that the habits from U10 are sticking. If it is not happening yet, go back to a simpler passing activity. The habit builds with repetition.

great_session.title: Players coaching each other
great_session.text: US Soccer notes this explicitly at U12: player-to-player coaching is a development goal, not just a nice thing to see. Step back when it happens.

great_session.title: Practice A concept in Practice B
great_session.text: If a concept introduced in the first session of the week appears in the second session without you asking for it, that is the whole point of two practices a week.

great_session.title: Everyone gets time in goal
great_session.text: Rotate the goalkeeper so every player experiences the position. If someone shows real enthusiasm for it, encourage that too. Positional identity starts forming at this age.

players.prepared: Preparation at U12 matters more than at any previous age. You have four active focuses and a season arc that builds deliberately. Know which focus is the priority for this week before you arrive. With two practices per week, Practice A introduces the concept and Practice B deepens it. If the group needs more time on the same concept before moving forward, run the consolidation instead. Both are correct responses. Try to avoid pairing two new concepts in the same session: Activity A works best as something players already know well enough to run without much explanation, and Activity B is where the new concept lives.

parents.outro: At this age players are more aware of what the sideline is saying than they were at U8 or U10. Positive sideline energy is genuinely useful. Critical sideline energy genuinely disrupts.

who.label: Growth is uneven
who.text: In any U14 group you will see players who have already grown a lot and players who have not started. Do not read size as skill. Praise decisions and effort, and watch that your biggest players are not only winning duels with size.

who.label: The field got big
who.text: The jump from 9v9 to 11v11 is a jump in distance, not just numbers. Players tire faster and shape breaks down. Short rests and water breaks are coaching tools, not weaknesses.

who.label: Peers matter more than you
who.text: At this age what teammates think carries a lot of weight. Individual feedback works best quietly, one on one. Public praise for team moments and brave decisions builds the culture you want.

who.label: Some will be ready for more

great_session.title: Players take the shot
great_session.text: The ball is in the final third and someone shoots, early, with composure, without a second dribble. Missing is fine. Not shooting is the problem.

great_session.title: Compact, connected shape
great_session.text: Eleven players on a big field can look scattered. Look for lines that stay close enough to support each other: defenders, midfielders and forwards moving as one unit.

great_session.title: Instant reaction on turnovers
great_session.text: When the ball changes hands, do players react in the first second or watch? That reaction is the whole game-moments block.

great_session.title: Players talking to each other

great_session.title: Practice A concept in Practice B

great_session.title: Everyone gets a turn in goal

B1.tagline: Prepare the body. Read the picture. Execute with intent.
B1.overview: Every player's relationship with the ball comes before everything else. This block establishes the perceptual and technical habits that make all combination play, defending and finishing possible: scanning before the ball arrives, shaping the body to play forward, and using first touch to create a decision rather than just react to pressure. When a player stalls in a later block, look back here first.

B2.tagline: Create advantage. Move the ball forward. Solve pressure together.
B2.overview: Combination play only works if the individual technique from the first block is already in place. This block takes that foundation and asks players to solve pressure together: recognizing a teammate's run, providing the right angle of support, and timing the next action so the advantage compounds rather than stalls.
B2.problem: Players use teammates to create time, space and numerical advantages, moving the ball forward under pressure through deliberate combination play.
focus: Combination play to break defensive lines
Movement after the pass, not just the pass itself

B3.tagline: Compact. Coordinated. Aggressive. Defending is not just for defenders.
B3.overview: Defending is not just for defenders. Winning the ball back is a collective action: the nearest player pressures, teammates cover behind, and the team stays connected and compact to protect dangerous space. The standard is no longer just reacting to losing the ball. Teams defend proactively, with a compact block that regains possession as high up the field as possible.
B3.problem: Players create and maintain a compact defensive block, applying coordinated pressure, cover and balance to prevent forward play and regain the ball.
focus: High defensive line and line management

B4.overview: Transitions are the moments that decide games. This block links attacking and defending: the instant possession changes, players must recognize the moment and respond, either with maximum intensity to win the ball back, or with immediate speed to attack before the opponent can organize. A player who reacts fast in transition is applying technique, combination and defensive shape all at once.
B4.problem: Players recognize the moment possession changes and respond immediately: pressing or recovering when it is lost, and playing forward at speed or securing the ball when it is won.
focus: Immediate recognition of the transition moment
Press or recover, play forward or secure

B5.tagline: Can we turn advantage into goals?
B5.overview: All of the work in the earlier blocks is preparation for this one. Players who scan early, combine well, defend collectively and transition fast create finishing opportunities. This block is about having the composure and technique to take them. When players struggle to finish, the answer is rarely more finishing drills. Check the quality of preparation touches, the timing of runs, and the decisions made before the shot.

routines.name: The Foundation
routines.objective: A daily ball mastery sequence each player does alone before group training. Ten moves, 20 reps of each, working in place.
routines.dosage: 20 reps of each move, every session

steps.name: Toe Taps
steps.how: Alternate light taps on top of the ball with each foot, staying on your toes.
steps.cue: Light contact, fast feet, ball barely moves.

steps.name: Foundations
steps.how: Tap the ball back and forth between the insides of your feet with short, controlled touches.
steps.cue: Stay light, keep a steady rhythm, keep the ball close.

steps.name: Sole Rolls
steps.how: Put one sole on the ball and roll it sideways to the other foot, which receives it and rolls it back.

steps.name: V-Pulls
steps.how: Pull the ball back with the sole, then push it diagonally forward with the inside of the same foot so it travels to the other foot in a V. That foot returns it the same way.
steps.cue: Sole pulls back, inside pushes the V forward.

steps.name: V-Pulls: Laces
steps.how: Same pattern as V-Pulls, but push forward with the laces instead of the inside.
steps.cue: Sole pulls back, laces push the V forward.

steps.name: La Croqueta
steps.how: Push the ball sideways with the inside of one foot and shift your whole body weight with it. The other foot receives it and pushes it back with another full weight shift.
steps.cue: Full weight shift. The body moves with the ball, not just the feet.

steps.name: Push Pull Laces
steps.how: Push forward with the laces, then pull back with the sole on the same foot. Keep touches short. Switch feet after your reps.
steps.cue: Laces push, sole pulls, stay balanced.

steps.name: Push Pull Insides
steps.how: Push across with the inside, then pull back with the sole on the same foot. Switch feet after your reps.
steps.cue: Inside pushes across, sole pulls back, stay light.

steps.name: Inside Outs
steps.how: Push the ball outside with the outside of your right foot, step over it, then push it back to center with the right inside. Repeat on the left. The step-over is part of the move.
steps.cue: Outside push, step over, inside back, other side. Keep the rhythm continuous.

steps.name: Elastico
steps.how: Push the ball outside with the outside of one foot, then flick it back inside with the inside of the same foot. Both touches are nearly simultaneous. Go slow until the touches are clean, then speed up.
steps.cue: Outside push, instant inside snap, one fluid move.
